claims.text: The test alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar mixing of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces significant local lattice distortions.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical disorder in WTaTiVZr activate additional dislocation slip systems.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical disorder in WTaTiVZr promote dynamic recovery.
Dislocation-mediated deformation operates in the TaTiVWZr refractory high-entropy alloy under temperature-dependent indentation creep loading.
Dislocations in TaTiVWZr become more thermally activated as temperature increases from 298 K to 573 K.
The proposed additional slip and dynamic recovery increase dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Enhanced dislocation mobility delays crack initiation and propagation under plasma-facing-component loading.
Relative to pure tungsten, loaded WTaTiVZr will exhibit increased dislocation mobility and activation of alternative slip systems.
Relative to pure tungsten, loaded WTaTiVZr will exhibit delayed crack initiation and propagation.
Pure tungsten has restricted high-temperature plasticity and earlier crack formation because it has fewer active slip systems than WTaTiVZr.
Matching grain size, initial defect density, and loading conditions between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten provides a controlled comparison.
High-energy X-ray diffraction and in situ imaging can quantitatively distinguish dislocation activity, slip-system activation, and crack evolution during the proposed high-temperature tests.
The hypothesis is limited to an equimolar alloy under temperatures, stresses, and strain rates representative of plasma-facing-component service.
